notes: Monday 19 Oct 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Fri 16 Oct through Sun 18 Oct (U.S./Europe time). Finance: Nasdaq’s worst week since June as AI chips slide; U.S. deficit near $2T; Europeans walk out on Russia at IMF Bangkok; Microsoft drops Essex AI data center over power. Tech (USA): Instagram downs No Kings account during rallies; Anthropic red team’s smart-TV AI worm; AI wearables vs wiretap laws; Musk settles $1M giveaway suits. Politics: France unrest (2,400 arrests); Trump pauses Russia sanctions, Starshield row; settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank; update—Homan says Omar could be denaturalized. Literature (USA): Allende wins Premio Planeta under a pen name; LitHub best-reviewed (Yiyun Li); horror-only bookstore; American Girl’s grown-up Samantha. Social: update—Oregon school shooting victims named; Canadian base fire kills 4; Kolkata Durga Puja crush; farmworker heat protections. Sources: Guardian, NPR, CNBC, BBC, Investopedia/Yahoo Finance, Literary Hub.

stories.headline: Nasdaq has its worst week since June as AI chip stocks keep sliding
stories.dek: Friday: Nasdaq −2.1%, S&P 500 −1.1%. Oil back above $100. Traders now see a December rate hike as very likely.
stories.caveman: U.S. stocks ended a rough week on Friday (Oct 16). The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 2.1% to 26,140, the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659, and the Dow slipped 0.3% to 52,002. For the week, the Nasdaq lost about 4.5%, its worst week since June; the S&P 500 lost about 2%, while the Dow actually rose 0.7%. Chip and AI stocks took the biggest hits: AI cloud company CoreWeave dropped about 12%, and Micron and Intel each fell more than 5%. Why? Investors are nervous that AI companies are borrowing huge amounts to build data centers, and that prices are still rising too fast. Fed chair Kevin Warsh gave no hint about rates in a speech, and futures markets put the chance of a rate hike in December at about 89%. The 10-year Treasury yield sat near 5.09%, and U.S. oil (WTI) jumped 3.4% to about $101 a barrel.
stories.why_it_matters: When a few giant AI stocks make up a big slice of the market, their slide drags down retirement funds for everyone. It also hit Asia: Taiwan’s market fell 4.47% last week, and the U.S. chip index’s weekly plunge points to more pressure on Monday.
stories.camps: Worried view: borrowing-fueled AI spending plus high oil and high rates is a fragile mix. Calmer view: the Dow rose for the week, showing money is rotating into other stocks rather than fleeing. Analyst Melissa Brown of SimCorp warned that when the top stocks are about 40% of the index, a pullback in them hits the whole market.
stories.image_alt: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange
stories.image_credit: Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images

terms.explain: A U.S. stock index full of tech companies.
An index of 500 big U.S. companies; a common measure of “the market.”
The interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow. Higher yields make loans pricier for everyone.
When the central bank raises interest rates to cool prices.
West Texas Intermediate, the main U.S. oil price benchmark.

stories.headline: U.S. budget gap hits nearly $2 trillion, the third-biggest ever
stories.dek: Spending was $7.4 trillion, tax money in was $5.4 trillion. Interest on the debt alone topped $1 trillion.
stories.caveman: The U.S. government spends more than it takes in. That gap is called the deficit. For the budget year that ended Sept. 30, the deficit was about $1.99 trillion, up 12% from $1.78 trillion the year before, CNBC reported (Oct 16). It is the third-largest deficit in U.S. history. The government took in about $5.4 trillion and spent about $7.4 trillion. Big costs: Social Security (about $1.7 trillion), Medicare (about $1.1 trillion), and interest on old debt (more than $1 trillion). Total national debt is now above $40 trillion. Money from corporate taxes fell by about $70 billion, partly because of tax cuts in the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” The government also had to refund about $145 billion in tariffs after a Supreme Court ruling, Reuters reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Paying over $1 trillion a year in interest means less money for schools, health care or anything else. Big deficits can also push interest rates up for mortgages and car loans.
stories.camps: Administration view: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the plan is to “grow our way out” of the debt with a faster economy. Critics’ view: budget watchers say tax cuts plus rising interest costs make the hole deeper, and someone will have to raise taxes or cut spending later.
stories.image_alt: A display showing the U.S. national debt in Washington, D.C.

terms.explain: How much more a government spends than it collects in one year.
All the money the government has borrowed over the years and not paid back.
The government’s budget year; for the U.S. it runs Oct. 1 to Sept. 30.
A tax on imported goods.

stories.headline: Bank of England chief and Europeans walk out on Russia’s finance minister at IMF meeting
stories.dek: Nearly half the room left when Anton Siluanov spoke in Bangkok; the U.S. said Russia should stay at the table.
stories.caveman: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is like a global emergency bank for countries. At its meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey and officials from France, Germany, Scandinavia and the Baltic states walked out when Russia’s finance minister, Anton Siluanov, started to speak, the Guardian reported (Oct 17). It was a protest over Russia’s war in Ukraine. Germany’s central bank chief Joachim Nagel said nearly half of the delegates left. The United States did not join; its representative supported Russia being present. The meeting’s chair, Saudi finance minister Mohammed al-Jadaan, warned that countries’ financial “buffers have been eroded” by years of shocks.
stories.why_it_matters: The walkout shows the West is split over how to treat Russia, as Washington takes a softer line. It also happened as the world economy faces high oil prices and war risks.
stories.camps: Walkout supporters: you shouldn’t give a stage to a country waging war on its neighbor. U.S. position: keep Russia in the room so talks can continue. Critics of the walkout argue global economic bodies work only if everyone can speak.
stories.image_alt: Delegates at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok

terms.explain: International Monetary Fund: lends to countries in trouble and watches the world economy.
A country’s main bank that sets interest rates, like the Bank of England.
Leaving a meeting on purpose as a protest.
Savings and safety cushions governments keep for bad times.

stories.headline: Microsoft drops huge AI data center near London because the power grid can’t deliver until the 2030s
stories.dek: The Essex site, planned with Nvidia-backed Nscale, couldn’t get electricity soon enough.
stories.caveman: AI needs giant buildings full of computers, called data centers, and they eat lots of electricity. Microsoft has pulled out of a planned AI data center at Loughton in Essex, near London, run by the British company Nscale, the Guardian reported (Oct 18). The local grid operator, UK Power Networks, could not supply enough power until the early-to-mid 2030s. The site was still being used as a scaffolding yard as recently as March. Nscale, which is backed by Nvidia and is reportedly eyeing a stock market listing at a valuation of about $35 billion, said it remains committed to the project. Microsoft is still working with Nscale on a project in Norway.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows the real limit on the AI boom isn’t only chips—it’s electricity. Countries that can’t build power lines fast enough may lose investment.
stories.camps: Pro-build view: the UK wants to be an AI hub and must speed up grid connections. Skeptical view: data centers strain power and water, and locals ask who benefits. Investors watch whether AI projects announced with fanfare actually get built.
stories.image_alt: Artist’s impression of the planned Nscale data center at Loughton, Essex (a rendering, not a photo)

terms.explain: A huge building full of computer servers that run apps and AI.
The network of power plants and lines that delivers electricity.
Initial public offering: when a company first sells shares on the stock market.

stories.headline: Instagram shuts down the No Kings protest account for hours during Saturday rallies
stories.dek: Meta says an automatic anti-bot system made a mistake; Democratic senators aren’t buying the timing.
stories.caveman: No Kings is a protest movement against President Trump. On Saturday (Oct 17), it held rallies tied to early voting, including at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, in Atlanta and in Los Angeles. During the protests, its Instagram account went offline for hours, the Guardian reported (Oct 18). Meta apologized. Spokesperson Andy Stone said bursts of very high activity made its AI tool mistake the account for bot traffic, that the automated action was “clearly taken in error,” and that the account was restored. Sen. Bernie Sanders blamed “billionaire ownership of the media,” and Sen. Chris Murphy called for an investigation.
stories.why_it_matters: A handful of tech companies control where Americans talk politics. Even an honest mistake at the wrong moment can silence a movement, which is why people demand transparency.
stories.camps: Meta’s view: automated systems remove millions of fake accounts, and errors happen and get fixed. Organizers’ and critics’ view: “Meta owes us an explanation,” the group said; a mistake that silences protesters at the worst moment raises censorship fears. Neutral point: there’s no public evidence yet that it was deliberate.
stories.image_alt: Demonstrators at a No Kings rally in New York

terms.explain: A U.S. protest movement opposing what it calls authoritarian moves by President Trump.
The company that owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
An automated fake account run by software.
Voting before Election Day at set locations.

stories.headline: Anthropic’s red team built an AI “worm” that hopped across smart TVs
stories.dek: The test showed AI could soon spread on its own across devices; experts say it could be possible within months.
stories.caveman: A “worm” is a computer virus that copies itself from one device to another by itself. AI company Anthropic’s red team—people hired to attack their own systems to find dangers—built an experimental AI worm that spread across smart TVs, even splitting its work across 15 TVs, the Guardian reported (Oct 18). The team says this kind of attack could become practical by the end of this year. Security veterans, including Joshua Saxe (formerly of Meta) and Chris Inglis (former deputy director of the NSA), told the paper that cheap internet-connected gadgets with weak security could become hiding places for AI attackers.
stories.why_it_matters: Your TV, doorbell or fridge may be the weakest door into your home network. AI that can spread on its own would make old security problems much bigger.
stories.camps: Alarmed view: AI makes hacking faster and cheaper, and gadget makers aren’t ready. Defenders’ view: testing it first is how you build defenses before criminals do. Skeptics say lab demos don’t always become real-world attacks quickly.
stories.image_alt: Televisions on display at an electronics show

terms.explain: Malware that spreads from device to device on its own.
Experts who attack their own organization’s systems to find weaknesses.
A TV connected to the internet that runs apps.
National Security Agency, the U.S. spy agency for electronic signals.

stories.headline: AI gadgets that record everything may run into old U.S. wiretap laws
stories.dek: New AI pins and watches summarize your day. In some states, recording people without consent can be illegal.
stories.caveman: A new wave of AI wearables listens all day and writes summaries for you. CNBC (Oct 18) points to Amazon’s new Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, launched last week, Apple Watch Series 12’s Siri “recap” feature, and Meta’s smart glasses. The problem: many U.S. states have wiretap laws that require everyone in a conversation to agree before it’s recorded. Massachusetts has an especially broad definition. Lawyer Colin Zick of Foley Hoag explained the legal risk, and Tufts University engineering professor Karen Panetta urged people to “embrace with caution.”
stories.why_it_matters: If your coworker’s pin is recording your lunch chat, your words may end up in a company’s cloud. Laws written for phone taps are now being tested by AI gadgets.
stories.camps: Makers’ view: these tools help memory, accessibility and productivity. Privacy view: people around you never agreed to be recorded. Legal view: the rules vary state by state, and courts haven’t settled how they apply.
stories.image_alt: Crowds of travelers in Moynihan Train Hall in New York

terms.explain: A gadget you wear, like a smartwatch, pin or glasses.
A law against secretly recording or listening to conversations.
Agreement or permission.

stories.headline: Musk settles lawsuits over his $1 million-a-day election giveaway
stories.dek: Plaintiffs said the 2024 swing-state “lottery” misled voters. Terms weren’t disclosed and need court approval.
stories.caveman: Before the 2024 election, Elon Musk’s America PAC handed out $1 million a day to people who signed a petition in seven swing states. Arizona residents later sued, saying voters were misled into signing by the promise of $1 million a day to “randomly selected” signers. Musk and the PAC have now settled two class-action lawsuits, the Guardian reported (Oct 17). The two proposed class actions were in federal court in Austin, Texas; the settlements still need a judge’s approval, and a judge had ordered Musk to testify in June. The settlement terms were not made public.
stories.why_it_matters: Very rich donors can reshape elections with giveaways like this. The settlement avoids a trial, so the public may never hear all the details.
stories.camps: Critics: the contest blurred the line between campaigning and paying voters. Musk’s side has argued the payments were legal, and a settlement isn’t an admission of wrongdoing.
stories.image_alt: Elon Musk and Donald Trump at an event on October 8, 2026
stories.image_credit: Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: Political action committee: a group that raises and spends money on elections.
One lawsuit filed on behalf of a whole group of people with the same complaint.
An agreement to end a lawsuit without a trial.
A state that could vote for either party.

stories.headline: France rocked by violent unrest: 2,400 arrested, a historic town hall set on fire
stories.dek: Student protests over schools have turned into riots; Macron condemns “unbridled violence.”
stories.caveman: France has seen four weeks of school marches and barricades by students demanding more teachers and repairs to run-down schools, joined by people angry about the cost of living. On Saturday some of it turned into the worst violence in years, the Guardian reported (Oct 18). At least 2,400 people have been arrested, including a record 855 in Paris. In Limoges, the 19th-century town hall was set on fire. President Emmanuel Macron called it “unbridled violence,” said “nothing justifies” it, and blamed the ultra-left and delinquents. Some politicians are calling for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign over the policing. Smaller protests have spread to Spain, Italy and Portugal. U.S. President Trump posted that France “is burning” and blamed immigrants, telling France to close its borders, Taiwan’s CNA reported from wire services.
stories.why_it_matters: The protests began with real complaints about schools. How the government answers—only with police, or also with fixes—could shape European politics for months.
stories.camps: Government: restore order first, punish violence. Peaceful protesters and the left: the anger comes from run-down schools and the cost of living; Macron himself separated peaceful marchers from looters. Right-wing voices: blame immigration and demand tougher policing; others say that framing ignores the original school protests.
stories.image_alt: The town hall in Limoges, France, on fire during unrest
stories.image_credit: Pascal Lachenaud / AFP / Getty Images (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: The French minister in charge of police and public order.
Far-left groups, some of which use street violence.
A violent public disturbance by a crowd.

stories.headline: Trump pauses new Russia sanctions and denies cutting Ukraine’s Starshield satellite link
stories.dek: Two days before a deadline, Trump used a national-interest waiver; Zelenskyy says the U.S. was behind a satellite outage.
stories.caveman: Congress passed a law (named after Sen. Lindsey Graham) to punish Russia with tougher sanctions. Two days before the deadline, President Trump signed an order pausing them, saying it was “in the national interest,” NPR reported (Oct 17–18). Sen. Richard Blumenthal accused him of “sucking up to Vladimir Putin.” Separately, Ukraine lost access to Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink satellite internet. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC the U.S. was behind it. Trump said “it wasn’t me,” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio called that “categorically false.” Musk said the U.S. military decides how the service can be used. Some senators want an inspector general to investigate. U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine has resumed, and Zelenskyy thanked Trump. Meanwhile Russia attacked overnight with 4 cruise missiles and 332 drones.
stories.why_it_matters: Ukraine’s army depends on U.S. intelligence and satellite internet to see and talk on the battlefield. Who controls that switch matters for the war.
stories.camps: White House: flexibility helps peace talks. Critics in both parties: pausing sanctions rewards Russia and weakens Congress’s law. Ukraine: grateful for renewed help but wants clear answers about the outage.
stories.image_alt: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at an EU summit

terms.explain: Penalties like trade bans meant to pressure another country.
SpaceX’s military satellite network, related to Starlink.
Official permission to skip a rule.
An internal watchdog that investigates a government agency.

stories.headline: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats and a French mayor in the West Bank
stories.dek: Three people were hurt in Taybeh during the olive harvest; even Trump’s ambassador called it terror.
stories.caveman: The West Bank is Palestinian land occupied by Israel, where Israeli settlers live in communities most of the world considers illegal. In the Palestinian village of Taybeh, settlers attacked a group that included France’s consul general, the Belgian and Polish consuls, French mayor Bernard Baudoux and the archbishop of Cambrai, who had come during the olive harvest, the Guardian reported (Oct 17). Three people were hurt, and a window of a Belgian armored car was smashed. Separately, Heidi Levine, a 63-year-old Washington Post photographer and U.S. citizen, was beaten late last week and needed surgery. U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee called it a “despicable act of terror,” while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu referred to it as an “alleged” attack. Israeli group Yesh Din counted more than 170 settler attacks since Sept. 27. Israel’s foreign minister condemned it and police are investigating; Belgium is pushing for EU sanctions on violent settlers.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on diplomats are rare and show how settler violence is rising during the olive harvest, when Palestinian farmers are most exposed.
stories.camps: Palestinians and rights groups: settlers act with little punishment, and the army often doesn’t stop them. Israeli government: condemns the attack and says police are investigating. European governments: want sanctions; the U.S. asked Israel to crack down.
stories.image_alt: The smashed window of mayor Baudoux’s car after the attack in Taybeh

terms.explain: Palestinian territory occupied by Israel since 1967.
Israelis living in communities built on occupied land.
A senior diplomat who represents a country in a city abroad.
An Israeli human-rights group that tracks settler violence.

stories.headline: Update: Trump’s border czar says Rep. Ilhan Omar could be stripped of citizenship and deported
stories.dek: After the Oct 12 search of her home, Tom Homan said “of course” it’s possible; Obama called it punishment for criticizing Trump.
stories.caveman: Last week federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home (our Oct 13 paper). New on Sunday: Trump’s border czar Tom Homan told Fox that “of course” Omar could be denaturalized—have her citizenship taken away—and deported, the Guardian reported (Oct 18). Former President Barack Obama said she was targeted “because she has dared to criticize the president,” and warned there is “no reason to believe it will stop with her.” Omar’s family fled Somalia’s civil war and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya; she became a citizen at 17 when her father was naturalized, and he filled out the paperwork. Her lawyers say the probe is election interference.
stories.why_it_matters: Taking citizenship away from a sitting member of Congress would be almost unheard of. Many naturalized citizens worry about what it would mean for them.
stories.camps: Administration: says it’s investigating possible fraud and no one is above the law. Omar, Democrats and civil-liberties groups: it’s political retaliation against a critic. Legal experts note denaturalization requires proving fraud in court and is hard to win.
stories.image_alt: Federal officers carry boxes from Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington residence on October 12
stories.image_credit: J. Scott Applewhite / AP (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: Taking away citizenship from someone who became a citizen later in life.
The White House official in charge of border and deportation policy.
Someone born abroad who became a citizen.

stories.headline: HOT: Isabel Allende, 84, wins Spain’s €1 million Premio Planeta under a secret pen name
stories.dek: She entered as “Luz Ventura” with a sequel to The House of the Spirits.
stories.caveman: Isabel Allende, the Chilean-American author whose books have sold more than 80 million copies, entered Spain’s richest literary contest under the fake name “Luz Ventura”—and won, the Guardian reported (Oct 17). The Premio Planeta pays €1 million. Her winning novel, La hora antes del alba (The Hour Before Dawn), continues The House of the Spirits, following Alba through Chile under the Pinochet dictatorship. Allende said winning felt “like winning the Nobel” and that she entered because she had “very little to lose.” Professor Duncan Wheeler of Leeds University said he’d be “very surprised” if the judges didn’t recognize her style, and called the Planeta generous but “definitely not the most prestigious.”
stories.why_it_matters: A U.S.-based literary superstar going back to her most famous world is big news for readers; an English translation is likely to be one of the most-watched releases.
stories.camps: Fans: a delightful twist—she proved herself again without her famous name. Skeptics: the pen name may not have fooled anyone, and the prize is seen as richer than it is prestigious.
stories.image_alt: Isabel Allende at the Premio Planeta ceremony
stories.image_credit: Pau de la Calle / GTRES / Shutterstock (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: A fake name an author writes under.
A Spanish literary prize run by publisher Planeta; one of the richest in the world.
A book that continues an earlier story.

stories.headline: HOT: Critics’ favorites this week—Yiyun Li’s Music Against the Night leads
stories.dek: LitHub’s roundup also features Bonnie Garmus, a new Eugene Debs biography and a book debunking longevity science.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub’s weekly list of the best-reviewed books (Oct 16) is led by Yiyun Li’s Music Against the Night, which one critic called “wonderful and bewitching.” Also on the list: Bonnie Garmus’s Peck & Peck, her follow-up to the giant hit Lessons in Chemistry; Shawn Gude’s American Socialist, about the labor leader Eugene Debs; and Saul Justin Newman’s Morbid, which debunks modern longevity science.
stories.why_it_matters: Review roundups help readers pick what’s worth their time and push books onto library hold lists and bookstore tables.
stories.camps: Fans: a strong week with a celebrated literary writer and a beloved bestseller. Skeptics: aggregate lists tend to reward books that got the most reviews, often from big publishers.
stories.image_alt: Book covers featured in LitHub’s best-reviewed books of the week

terms.explain: Books that professional critics praised most this week.
An American labor leader and five-time Socialist presidential candidate in the early 1900s.
Bonnie Garmus’s 2022 bestselling debut novel.

stories.headline: HOT: Horror is booming—and now there’s a bookstore that sells only scary books
stories.dek: Long Dark House in Alexandria, Virginia, opened about a month ago as horror sales climb.
stories.caveman: Chanthal Harris used to work in aviation. Now she runs Long Dark House, a bookstore in Alexandria, Virginia, that sells only horror, NPR reported (Oct 18). It opened about a month ago, right before Halloween season. Horror is hot: NPR cited Nielsen market research showing the genre’s profits up almost 26% year over year, and the horror movie Backrooms made more than $400 million on a $10 million budget.
stories.why_it_matters: Small specialty bookstores are a sign of what readers are excited about. Horror readers are often young and active on social media, which helps books spread.
stories.camps: Fans: horror lets people face fear safely and talk about real anxieties. Business skeptics: a one-genre shop is a risky bet if the trend cools.
stories.image_alt: Inside Long Dark House, a horror bookstore in Alexandria, Virginia

terms.explain: A category of books, like horror, romance or mystery.
A company that tracks book sales and media audiences.
An independently owned bookshop, not part of a chain.

stories.headline: American Girl turns 40 with a grown-up Samantha novel by Fiona Davis
stories.dek: In Samantha: The Next Chapter, the doll’s heroine is 25 in 1920—“from socialite to shopgirl.”
stories.caveman: American Girl dolls come with history books about girls from different eras. For the brand’s 40th birthday, bestselling author Fiona Davis wrote Samantha: The Next Chapter, NPR reported (Oct 18). The original Samantha was a rich orphan in 1904; now she is 25 years old in 1920 and goes “from socialite to shopgirl.” NPR also recalled that Addy Walker, added in 1993, was the brand’s first nonwhite doll.
stories.why_it_matters: Many adults grew up with these books. Writing grown-up sequels is a way publishers bring nostalgic readers back.
stories.camps: Fans: a sweet way for 1990s kids to reunite with a childhood hero. Critics: brands increasingly sell nostalgia; some wonder whether it’s more marketing than literature.
stories.image_alt: Author Fiona Davis

terms.explain: A warm longing for the past.
Novels set in a real past period.
A wealthy person known for going to fancy social events.

stories.headline: Update: Oregon school shooting—victims named, a father stopped the attacker
stories.dek: At Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, three children and a teacher were killed; a teacher wrestled the gunman before an armed father shot him.
stories.caveman: New details on the shooting we reported Friday. At Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, a 16-year-old former student killed three children and a teacher, the BBC reported (Oct 17). A teacher tried to wrestle the gun away, and a father of two students at the school, who was driving past and was armed, ran inside and shot him dead. Two of the dead were named as Rhoam Summer, 5, and teacher Meghan Lambert, 25. A 54-year-old teacher and a 7-year-old child were injured. Police said he carried about 44 more rounds of ammunition.
stories.why_it_matters: School shootings remain a uniquely American crisis. Every case restarts the debate over guns and school safety.
stories.camps: Gun-rights view: an armed bystander saved lives. Gun-safety view: a 16-year-old should never have had a gun, and stronger laws (like safe storage) would prevent the attack in the first place. Everyone: mourning the children and the teachers who acted.
stories.image_alt: Mourners leave flowers near Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon

terms.explain: Someone who used to attend the school.
A law requiring guns to be locked away from children.
Bullets.

stories.headline: Fast grass fire and explosion at Canadian army base kill four soldiers
stories.dek: At CFB Wainwright in Alberta, the fire moved “a kilometre in 36 seconds”; 39 are in hospital.
stories.caveman: A grass fire swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, followed by an explosion, the Guardian reported (Oct 18). Officials said the fire moved “a kilometre in 36 seconds.” Four soldiers were killed: Sgt. Morgan Wong and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark. Thirty-nine people were taken to hospital, 19 in critical condition. Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered flags at half-mast, and the RCMP is investigating.
stories.why_it_matters: It’s one of the deadliest training accidents for Canada’s military in years, and questions about safety on the base will follow.
stories.camps: Military: grieving and promising answers. Families and safety experts: want to know whether the fire risk was known and why people couldn’t get away. The investigation hasn’t found a cause yet.
stories.image_alt: Emergency vehicles near CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.image_credit: John Ulan / The Canadian Press / AP (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: Canadian Forces Base, a Canadian military base.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Canada’s national police.
Flying a flag halfway down the pole to show mourning.

stories.headline: Crowd crush at Durga Puja festival in Kolkata kills at least 17
stories.dek: Rain and a loudspeaker announcement set off a stampede; a 7-year-old girl is among the dead.
stories.caveman: Durga Puja is one of the biggest Hindu festivals, with huge crowds visiting decorated pavilions. In Kolkata, India, a crowd crush killed at least 17 people, including a 7-year-old girl, and injured 25, the BBC reported (Oct 17). Officials said rain and an announcement caused people to rush. West Bengal’s chief minister, named by the BBC as Suvendhu Adhikari, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi called it tragic. Two years ago, 121 people died in a crush at a religious event in Uttar Pradesh.
stories.why_it_matters: Crowd crushes keep happening at big religious gatherings in India. Better crowd control can save lives.
stories.camps: Officials: express grief and promise help for families. Safety experts: say organizers need limits on numbers, more exits and clear communication, and that such disasters are preventable.
stories.image_alt: Police and a Kolkata Traffic Police ambulance surrounded by onlookers after the crowd crush
stories.image_credit: AFP via Getty Images (via BBC News)

terms.explain: When a packed crowd pushes so hard that people can’t breathe or fall and get trampled.
A major Hindu festival, especially big in West Bengal.
The elected head of an Indian state government.

stories.headline: After America’s hottest summer, farmworkers point to a program that actually protects them from heat
stories.dek: The Fair Food Program makes big buyers like Walmart and McDonald’s demand heat breaks; federal rules are stuck.
stories.caveman: This past summer was the hottest on record in the U.S., and farmworkers pick crops in that heat. The Guardian (Oct 18) reports that many advocates see the Coalition of Immokalee Workers’ Fair Food Program as the model: 14 retailers, including Walmart, McDonald’s, Whole Foods and Trader Joe’s, agree to buy only from farms that give shade, water and breaks. Another group, WeCount, is pressuring plant grower Costa Farms. Meanwhile, Florida banned cities from passing their own heat rules, a national OSHA heat standard has stalled, and Rep. Mark Messmer has a bill that would block it.
stories.why_it_matters: Heat kills workers every year. When governments don’t act, buyer pressure may be the only protection workers get.
stories.camps: Workers’ advocates: heat rules are basic safety and should be law. Business groups and some Republicans: one-size-fits-all rules are costly and states should decide. Middle ground: voluntary programs work for some farms but cover only part of the workforce.

The U.S. agency for workplace safety.
When a higher government (like a state) blocks lower ones (like cities) from making their own rules.
